entries.description: A Valentine's greeting, spelled out in full or in some variation on it, is written into the picture in any language. Chocolate and hearts without the lettering do not qualify.

entries.name: graffiti
entries.description: Writing or drawings sprayed or painted on a wall, shutter, [train](#train) or another public surface, usually stylised and unsanctioned. Common in [street](#street) and [urban](#urban) backgrounds.

entries.name: trick_or_treat
entries.description: The phrase Trick or Treat, or a close variation of it, written somewhere on the picture, usually alongside Halloween artwork. The act of going [door](#door) to door is [trick-or-treating](#trick-or-treating), and the holiday itself is [halloween](#halloween).

entries.name: akeome
entries.description: The shortened Japanese New Year greeting written into the picture, [standing](#standing) for the longer formal phrase. Use it where the words themselves appear, not for every New Year scene.

entries.name: qr_code
entries.description: A [square](#square) matrix [barcode](#barcode) of black modules on a white [field](#field) appears somewhere in the picture, most often encoding a web address. It may be a [working](#working) code or purely decorative.

entries.name: yes
entries.description: The word 'yes' is written prominently in the picture as emphasis, whether on a [sign](#sign), a [pillow](#pillow) or [floating](#floating) text. A [yes-no_pillow](#yes-no_pillow) showing its yes side takes this [tag](#tag) too.

entries.name: group_name
entries.description: The name of a team, band, unit or other character grouping appears as text in the picture. Not [circle_name](#circle_name), which names an artist [circle](#circle).

entries.name: lyrics
entries.description: Song lyrics written into the picture, as a [caption](#caption), inside a speech [bubble](#bubble) or as decorative text across the background. The words themselves are what the [tag](#tag) records.

entries.name: warning_sign
entries.description: A [caution](#caution) [sign](#sign), usually a [triangle](#triangle) with an exclamation mark, marking danger. Specific hazard marks such as the biohazard, radiation or skull-and-crossbones symbols have their own tags.

entries.name: wall_of_text
entries.description: A large dense block of [writing](#writing) fills part of the picture, often the background or a page. The text is a visual mass rather than a [caption](#caption) or dialogue.

entries.name: keep_out
entries.description: The words keep out appear somewhere in the picture, most often on barrier [tape](#tape), a [sign](#sign) or a boarded [doorway](#doorway). Tag the tape or sign as an object as [well](#well).

entries.name: kotoyoro
entries.description: The written second half of the customary New Year greeting, asking for continued goodwill through the coming year. Use it when those words are actually drawn into the picture, not merely when the season is.

entries.name: hashtag
entries.description: A word or phrase run together behind a hash [sign](#sign), the way topics are labelled online. It appears as written text somewhere in the picture — on a [screen](#screen), a [placard](#placard), a [caption](#caption) strip.

entries.name: congratulations
entries.description: A written message of congratulation appears in the picture, as lettering across the art or on a [banner](#banner) or [card](#card) inside it. Birthdays, anniversaries, victories and milestones are the usual occasions.

entries.name: price_tag
entries.description: A small [label](#label) or [sticker](#sticker) attached to goods to show what they cost. Sometimes hung on a character as a joke about being for [sale](#sale).

entries.name: food_name
entries.description: The name of a dish or ingredient appears written in the picture, on a [menu](#menu), a [sign](#sign), a wrapper or a [label](#label). It is text about [food](#food) rather than the food itself.

entries.name: ai_ai_gasa
entries.description: Two names written under a sketched [umbrella](#umbrella), one on either side of the [handle](#handle), as a piece of lovers' [graffiti](#graffiti). It plays the part that [carving](#carving) initials inside a [heart](#heart) does elsewhere. Two [people](#people) genuinely [sharing](#sharing) an umbrella is [shared_umbrella](#shared_umbrella).

entries.name: game_over
entries.description: The words announcing that a game has ended in [defeat](#defeat), usually set large over a [dark](#dark) [field](#field). Used both in straight game imagery and as a joke about a character being [beaten](#beaten).

entries.name: vehicle_name
entries.description: The name of a specific vehicle is lettered somewhere in the picture, on a hull, fuselage or bodywork. Misspellings, alternate renderings and abbreviations still count, but a generic class word such as [tank](#tank) or [car](#car) does not.

entries.name: happy_anniversary
entries.description: The words "Happy Anniversary" appear written into the picture, in English or in any other [tongue](#tongue). Other set greetings such as [birthday](#birthday) wishes, thanks or [congratulations](#congratulations) have their own tags.

entries.name: underwear_writing
entries.description: Lettering runs along the elastic waistband of [underwear](#underwear) or the band of a sports [bra](#bra), in the manner of a designer-brand pair. Text printed on the [fabric](#fabric) of an ordinary garment belongs under [clothes_writing](#clothes_writing) instead.

entries.name: error_message
entries.description: A [failure](#failure) notice on a [screen](#screen), [window](#window) or terminal, often with a warning icon and a button to dismiss it. Usually drawn with [glitch](#glitch) effects, or as a joke about something going wrong.

entries.name: glass_writing
entries.description: Letters traced with a fingertip through [fog](#fog) on a [window](#window) or a [mirror](#mirror). Text drawn this way often comes out reversed when the writer forgets which side it will be read from.

entries.name: initial
entries.description: A name cut down to one or a few letters and shown somewhere in the picture. Monograms, badges, signs and marks on clothing are where it appears.

entries.name: sign_around_neck
entries.description: A [placard](#placard) hung from a cord over someone's [neck](#neck) so the [writing](#writing) faces the viewer. Used for shaming, [begging](#begging) or [confession](#confession) jokes, and usually carries a short handwritten message.

entries.name: weapon_name
entries.description: A weapon's name appears written somewhere in the picture, with that [weapon](#weapon) also visible. Typical of presentation art and game-style stat cards.

entries.name: album_name
entries.description: The [title](#title) of a [music](#music) release is written into the picture, on a mock sleeve, a poster or a [shop](#shop) [display](#display). The lettering is part of what the picture shows.

entries.name: no
entries.description: The word no is written in the picture and carries the point or the joke. The lettering has to be visible; a refusal merely acted out does not count.

entries.name: exit_sign
entries.description: A [sign](#sign) marking the way out, either the [plain](#plain) word or the green lit pictogram of a [running](#running) [figure](#figure). Mounted above doors and along corridors.

entries.name: vs
entries.description: The letters VS appear directly in the picture, signalling a matchup between two or more competitors. It borrows the look of a [fighting](#fighting) game's pre-match [announcement](#announcement) [screen](#screen) and should only be used when that lettering is actually visible.

entries.name: mirrored_text
entries.description: Lettering reversed left to right, as though painted on [glass](#glass) and read from the far side. Distinct from text that runs backwards word by word or hangs upside down.

entries.name: caution
entries.description: The word CAUTION is printed somewhere in the picture, on [tape](#tape), a [sign](#sign) or a barrier fencing something off. It records the lettering itself, not a general sense of danger.

entries.name: acronym
entries.description: An abbreviation built from the [initial](#initial) letters of a longer name is written into the picture. Real-world ones and invented in-setting ones both qualify.

entries.name: hand_fan_writing
entries.description: Characters, slogans or names lettered across the [paper](#paper) face of a folding or rigid hand fan. The text belongs to the fan itself, not to a [sign](#sign) or the background behind it.

entries.name: dying_message
entries.description: A last message scrawled by somebody as they die, classically in their own [blood](#blood), naming the killer or leaving a clue. A fixture of [murder](#murder) mystery imagery.

entries.name: impact_(font)
entries.description: The [heavy](#heavy) condensed typeface used for caption-over-picture jokes, most often white with a black [outline](#outline) along the top or bottom edge. Its presence alone signals a joke [caption](#caption).

entries.name: propaganda
entries.description: Imagery built around promoting a political, national, or ideological cause: a slogan as the whole point of the picture, praise for a leader or movement, or a [parody](#parody) of either. Slogans printed on a character's clothing count too, and this is distinct from ordinary commercial advertising.

entries.name: height_mark
entries.description: Graduated lines and figures on a wall, a doorframe or a board for [measuring](#measuring) how [tall](#tall) somebody is. Familiar from a family's [record](#record) of a growing [child](#child) and from [police](#police) booking backdrops.

entries.name: i_heart...
entries.description: Wording of the form "I ♥ something" written somewhere in the picture. It is printed across the front of a [shirt](#shirt) more often than anywhere else.

entries.name: tweet
entries.description: A social-media post drawn into the picture complete with [handle](#handle), avatar and message [box](#box). Often used to frame a joke or give a character an in-world remark.

entries.name: food_writing
entries.description: Words written onto the [food](#food) itself, iced across a [cake](#cake) or squeezed in [ketchup](#ketchup) over an omelette. Text on the packaging is a separate matter, and [writing](#writing) on skin is [body_writing](#body_writing).

entries.name: happy_holidays
entries.description: The phrase "Happy Holidays" is written into the picture. Although intended as a broader seasonal greeting, in practice it shows up almost entirely on Christmas art.

entries.name: mvp
entries.description: The three letters MVP written somewhere in the picture, naming the standout player of a match or a season. Tag it where the lettering itself is shown, on a [trophy](#trophy), a [banner](#banner) or a [shirt](#shirt).

entries.name: danmaku_comments
entries.description: Viewer comments streaming across the picture from right to left, [imitating](#imitating) the overlay used by [video](#video) sites such as Niconico and Bilibili. At a big moment they [pile](#pile) up thickly enough to bury what lies underneath.

entries.name: mug_writing
entries.description: Words or a slogan printed anywhere on a [mug](#mug) in the picture, whether it is held, [standing](#standing) on a [desk](#desk) or being [drunk](#drunk) from. Names, slogans and joke captions are the usual content.

entries.name: convention_greeting
entries.description: The customary thank-you message an artist writes into a picture once an event has ended, naming the gathering. It closes out the event rather than describing the scene.

entries.name: news
entries.description: A news broadcast on a [screen](#screen), or a headline and [article](#article) in a [paper](#paper) or magazine, appearing inside the picture. Invented reports count as readily as real ones.

entries.name: command_input
entries.description: The button sequence for a special move in a [video](#video) game is drawn onto the picture, either as arrow and button icons or in [numbered](#numbered) shorthand. Almost always a fighting-game reference.

entries.name: plant_name
entries.description: The name of a [plant](#plant) written somewhere in the picture, on a [label](#label), a [sign](#sign), or a [caption](#caption). Only the [writing](#writing) itself counts, not the plant shown alongside it.

entries.name: foreground_text
entries.description: Writing laid over everything else in the image, opaque and plainly in front of the scene. Unlike a [watermark](#watermark) it is meant to be read as part of the picture.

entries.name: headwear_writing
entries.description: Text on headwear of any kind: a slogan across a cap, characters brushed on a [headband](#headband), a word knitted into a [beanie](#beanie).

entries.name: label
entries.description: A printed slip or [sticker](#sticker) fixed to an object to say what it is, as on a [bottle](#bottle), [jar](#jar), [box](#box) or parcel. The wording it carries is usually the reason it is drawn at all.

entries.name: poem
entries.description: Verse written into the picture, set out in [broken](#broken) lines rather than as ordinary prose. The words themselves are part of the artwork, whether inked by hand, printed, or unrolled on a [scroll](#scroll).

entries.name: scientific_name
entries.description: The Latin binomial of a species written somewhere in the image, usually as a [caption](#caption) set beside the [creature](#creature) it names.

entries.name: blood_writing
entries.description: Letters or symbols written in [blood](#blood) on a wall, a [floor](#floor), [paper](#paper) or skin. The message has to be legible; a random smear is not this.

entries.name: achievement_unlocked
entries.description: The pop-up [banner](#banner) a games console throws up when a [trophy](#trophy) is earned, laid over the scene. It is nearly always a joke about something mundane [counting](#counting) as an accomplishment.

entries.name: writing_on_wall
entries.description: Lettering painted, scrawled or scratched directly onto a wall within the scene, such as [graffiti](#graffiti), a warning or a message left for someone. The wall surface itself carries the text, rather than a [sign](#sign), poster or [note](#note) [pinned](#pinned) to it.

entries.name: happy_easter
entries.description: The Easter greeting appears lettered somewhere in the picture, in English or in another [tongue](#tongue). The text itself is what matters, not the eggs and rabbits around it.

entries.name: chalkboard_sign
entries.description: A slate panel in a frame, written on in [chalk](#chalk) and stood outside a [shop](#shop) or [cafe](#cafe). Handwritten menus and drawn [decorations](#decorations) fill it.

entries.name: button_prompt
entries.description: A [controller](#controller) button icon drawn into the picture the way a [video](#video) game displays one, cueing an action. It comes with game screenshots and interface parodies.

entries.name: nameplate
entries.description: A rigid [plate](#plate) bearing a name, [standing](#standing) [folded](#folded) on a [desk](#desk) or fixed beside a front [door](#door). Unlike a [cloth](#cloth) name [tag](#tag) it belongs to the place rather than to a person's [clothes](#clothes).

entries.name: hat_writing
entries.description: Letters, words or numbers printed, [stitched](#stitched) or scrawled across a [hat](#hat). Slogan [baseball](#baseball) caps are the usual case.

entries.name: animal_name
entries.description: A creature's common name is written somewhere in the picture, in any language. The Latin binomial belongs to the scientific-name [tag](#tag) rather than here.

entries.name: free_hugs
entries.description: A hand-lettered [sign](#sign) offering embraces to passing strangers, held up in a public place. It comes from the [street](#street) campaign of that name, and the [hug](#hug) itself may or may not be happening.

entries.name: open_sign
entries.description: The [placard](#placard) hung in a [shop](#shop) or [restaurant](#restaurant) [window](#window) telling passers-by that the business is [serving](#serving). Often being turned around or carried by somebody starting a shift.

entries.name: speed_limit_sign
entries.description: A roadside [sign](#sign) stating the maximum permitted speed. Japanese, European, and Russian versions are typically a [plain](#plain) number ringed in red, while American signs are white rectangles with wording set above the [figure](#figure).

entries.name: not_for_sale
entries.description: Printed matter in the picture, such as a [card](#card), a [book](#book) or a [cover](#cover) page, carries wording stating that it is not being sold.

entries.name: good_morning
entries.description: The English words Good Morning written somewhere in the picture, usually greeting the viewer beside a character just out of [bed](#bed). The words have to be visible; a waking-up scene alone does not count.

entries.name: place_name
entries.description: The name of a place, real or invented, written somewhere in the picture: on a signboard, a [map](#map), or a [caption](#caption). Only the written name counts, not any depiction of the place itself.

entries.name: episode_title
entries.description: The name of an episode appears as lettering in the picture, usually on a [title](#title) [card](#card) laid over a scene. It often sits next to the episode number.
The web error for a page that cannot be found appears in the picture. It shows up as an error [screen](#screen) or as a joke about something missing where it should be.

entries.name: plaque
entries.description: A flat mounted [plate](#plate) [carrying](#carrying) an inscription, an award, or a memorial text, fixed to a wall or [standing](#standing) on a base. The lettering is usually the whole reason it appears in the picture.

entries.name: level_up
entries.description: The phrase level up, or a close variation of it, is written into the picture, borrowing a game's progress notice. Usually a joke about a character gaining strength or skill.

entries.name: wet_floor_sign
entries.description: The folding yellow [triangle](#triangle) set out to warn that a [floor](#floor) is slippery. It usually shows a [slipping](#slipping) [figure](#figure) alongside a line of text.

entries.name: rest_in_peace_(phrase)
entries.description: The words rest in peace appearing somewhere in the image, including the shortened R.I.P. and the Latin requiescat in pace. Often written on a gravestone or as a [caption](#caption) over a mock memorial.

entries.name: english_text
entries.description: The [writing](#writing) in the picture is mainly English — dialogue, signs, captions. Passing English such as an artist's name, a [signature](#signature), a web address or a [watermark](#watermark) does not count; speech bubbles are the usual cue.

entries.name: chinese_text
entries.description: Chinese [writing](#writing) appears somewhere in the picture, in either traditional or simplified characters. Japanese kanji on its own does not count and takes japanese_text instead.

entries.name: korean_text
entries.description: Korean [writing](#writing) appears somewhere in the picture, almost always in the Hangul [alphabet](#alphabet), occasionally as Chinese characters or a romanised spelling. Combine it with [speech_bubble](#speech_bubble) or [sign](#sign) as the placement requires.

entries.name: ranguage
entries.description: Text in a foreign language written with mistakes by a non-native [speaker](#speaker), typically Japanese attempts at French, German, or Finnish that carry spelling or grammar errors. Mangled English specifically has its own more common [tag](#tag), engrish.

entries.name: engrish_text
entries.description: English written by somebody who does not speak it [well](#well), with mangled grammar, spelling or word [choice](#choice). Almost always unintentional in the original artwork.

entries.name: romaji_text
entries.description: Japanese written in the Latin [alphabet](#alphabet) where Japanese [script](#script) would be expected, such as dialogue or [sound](#sound) effects. Names and brand names already in Latin letters do not count, nor do words adopted into English like [sushi](#sushi).

entries.name: mixed-language_text
entries.description: Text in two or more languages appearing within the same picture, such as Japanese dialogue set beside an English [caption](#caption).

entries.name: russian_text
entries.description: Text in the Russian language appearing in the picture, written in Cyrillic [script](#script). Tag alongside other language tags when several appear together.

entries.name: simplified_chinese_text
entries.description: Written Chinese in the simplified character set appears in the picture. Tag alongside [chinese_text](#chinese_text); [traditional_chinese_text](#traditional_chinese_text) covers the other [script](#script).

entries.name: runes
entries.description: Characters from historical runic alphabets or similar invented symbols, carved on stones, [glowing](#glowing) in [magic](#magic) circles or written on a page. Tag as text instead where it forms legible [writing](#writing).

entries.name: german_text
entries.description: Writing in German somewhere in the picture, as dialogue, signage or a [caption](#caption).

entries.name: black_text
entries.description: Writing in the picture set in black [ink](#ink). It covers any lettering that reads black, from signs and captions to lines of dialogue.

entries.name: furigana
entries.description: Small kana printed beside kanji to show how they are read, a form of ruby text. Worth tagging because it settles the pronunciation of names and words for anyone [reading](#reading) the picture.

entries.name: bilingual
entries.description: The same words appear twice in two languages, such as Japanese speech with an English rendering beside it. The second version is not necessarily a faithful translation.

entries.name: spanish_text
entries.description: Writing in the Spanish language appears somewhere in the picture, whether as dialogue, a [caption](#caption), or signage. Covers Spanish from Spain, Latin America, or anywhere else it is spoken.

entries.name: thai_text
entries.description: Writing in the Thai [script](#script) appears somewhere in the picture.

entries.name: cursive
entries.description: Joined-up handwriting somewhere in the picture, whether a [signature](#signature), a [letter](#letter) or decorative [script](#script). Add the [tag](#tag) for the language the text is in.

entries.name: bilingual_text
entries.description: Writing in two different languages [sharing](#sharing) one picture, for instance Japanese lettering next to English. Add the tags for each of the languages present as [well](#well).

entries.name: french_text
entries.description: Writing in the French language somewhere in the picture, as dialogue, a [sign](#sign) or a [caption](#caption). Tag the other languages present as [well](#well) where a picture mixes them.

entries.name: traditional_chinese_text
entries.description: Writing set in Traditional Chinese characters, as used in Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau rather than the simplified forms used on the mainland.

entries.name: italian_text
entries.description: Writing in Italian appears in the frame, as dialogue, a [caption](#caption) or a [sign](#sign). It records what language is written, not Italian [food](#food), places or characters.

entries.name: emoticon
entries.description: A face built out of punctuation and letters, read [sideways](#sideways) like :) or upright like [^_^](#^_^). It is written as characters inside the picture, not drawn as an expression on anybody's face.

entries.name: cyrillic
entries.description: Lettering in the Cyrillic [alphabet](#alphabet) appears somewhere in the picture, the [script](#script) written for Russian and for many Slavic and Central Asian languages. Several letters resemble Latin ones but [sound](#sound) different, and others have [no](#no) Latin counterpart at all.

entries.name: hieroglyphics
entries.description: Picture-writing set out in rows of birds, eyes and small figures, most often the Egyptian sort. It appears carved into walls and stelae or inked onto scrolls and props.

entries.name: kansaiben
entries.description: The dialogue is written in the dialect of the Kansai region, with its own verb endings, particles and vocabulary. Translators often stand it in for a regional drawl.

entries.name: latin_text
entries.description: Writing in the Latin language appears somewhere in the picture. Magic circles, [heraldry](#heraldry) and [church](#church) settings account for most of it.

entries.name: kunreishiki
entries.description: Japanese romanised by the scheme taught in Japanese schools, which follows the kana [grid](#grid) rather than English sounds and so yields spellings like si and sya. The alternative Hepburn system writes the same syllables shi and sha.

entries.name: greek_text
entries.description: Greek letters written somewhere in the picture, on a [sign](#sign), a page, an inscription or a spoken line. The [alphabet](#alphabet) is what identifies it, whatever the words say.

entries.name: finnish_text
entries.description: Writing in Finnish appears somewhere in the picture, on a [sign](#sign), in speech or as a [caption](#caption). Only the language is at issue, not what the words say.

entries.name: indonesian_text
entries.description: Writing in the Indonesian language somewhere in the picture. It uses Latin letters and grew out of Malay, so it is easily mistaken for Malaysian.

entries.name: kaomoji
entries.description: An [emoticon](#emoticon) built out of typed characters and read the right way up, such as (・∀・). It appears in dialogue, on screens, or [floating](#floating) beside a character in place of a drawn expression.

entries.name: h_(letter)
entries.description: The character H drawn somewhere in the image, as an [initial](#initial), a [logo](#logo) or a lone [letter](#letter). In Japanese material it frequently stands for "ecchi" and carries a lewd joke.

entries.name: multilingual
entries.description: One picture carries the same wording in three or more languages. Whether the translations are any good is a separate question; only the number of languages matters.

entries.name: portuguese_text
entries.description: Writing in Portuguese somewhere in the image, as dialogue, signage or a [caption](#caption). Covers both the European and the Brazilian varieties.

entries.name: ze_(phrase)
entries.description: A masculine, emphatic Japanese sentence-ending particle given visual prominence, either filling a speech [bubble](#bubble) by itself or spelled out in the Latin [alphabet](#alphabet). Ordinary use of the particle inside a longer sentence does not count.

entries.name: hiroshimaben
entries.description: Dialogue written in the western Japanese dialect associated with [gangster](#gangster) films, with its own copula and sentence-final particles. Translations often render it as a broad [rural](#rural) accent.

entries.name: vietnamese_text
entries.description: Writing in Vietnamese somewhere in the picture, recognisable by Latin letters loaded with stacked accent marks. Signs, captions and dialogue all count.

entries.name: blackletter
entries.description: Angular [medieval](#medieval) European lettering with [heavy](#heavy) strokes and [ornate](#ornate) hooks, also called Gothic [script](#script) or Fraktur. It turns up on certificates, mastheads and metal band logos; use it for the letterforms, not for the language written in them.

entries.name: seal_script
entries.description: An archaic, squared-off style of Chinese characters. Seen carved into name seals and used wherever an antique flavour is wanted.

entries.name: arabic_text
entries.description: Writing in the Arabic [script](#script) somewhere in the picture, on signs, in speech, as [calligraphy](#calligraphy) or in the background. Persian and Kurdish use related scripts and have separate tags.

entries.name: siddham
entries.description: An [old](#old) Indic [script](#script) once used to write Sanskrit mantras and [seed](#seed) syllables. Appears on talismans, banners and [magic](#magic) imagery as rounded ornamental characters.

entries.name: nonstandard_furigana
entries.description: The small kana printed beside kanji give an unexpected [reading](#reading), so what is written and what is said pull apart for [comic](#comic) or poetic effect. Japanese calls such a reading gikun.

entries.name: alphabet
entries.description: The letters of a [writing](#writing) system set out in their proper order, as a [chart](#chart), poster or blackboard. The sequence itself is the content, not a word spelled with it.

entries.name: kanji_focus
entries.description: Chinese characters carry the picture, blown up as its central design or set out to be read. The lettering is the subject rather than an incidental [sign](#sign) in the background.

entries.name: swedish_text
entries.description: Writing in the Swedish language appears somewhere in the picture, whether in a speech [bubble](#bubble), on a [sign](#sign) or as a [caption](#caption).

entries.name: gradient_text
entries.description: Lettering filled with a colour that shifts across the glyphs instead of one flat fill. A fade between two greys counts as readily as one between hues.

entries.name: orange_text
entries.description: Lettering appearing in the picture is rendered in orange.

entries.name: brown_text
entries.description: Lettering in the picture set in brown [ink](#ink). Any [writing](#writing) counts, from a scrawled [note](#note) to printed dialogue.
The year 2023 is written somewhere in the image or referred to, for instance on a Year of the Rabbit [card](#card). The date the work was finished does not count.
The figures 2024 appear as text or the scene clearly refers to that year, which fell under the Dragon. A picture merely drawn in 2024 is not tagged.
The year 2022 appears as lettering or as a [plain](#plain) reference, often a Year of the Tiger greeting. Pictures made that year without saying so do not qualify.
The figures 2016 appear as text or the scene alludes to that year, which fell under the Monkey. Pictures that only date from 2016 do not qualify.
The number 2021 is written into the picture or referred to by its content, as on a Year of the Ox [card](#card). Do not apply it for the creation date alone.
The year 2017 is written into the image or referred to, for example on a Year of the Rooster [card](#card). When the picture was drawn has [no](#no) bearing on it.

entries.name: tally
entries.description: Counting marks drawn somewhere in the picture: four strokes crossed by a fifth in the Western style, or the character 正 built up stroke by stroke in the East Asian [convention](#convention).
The year 2015 is written in the picture or referenced by its content, as on a Year of the Goat [card](#card). It is not for [recording](#recording) when the work was made.
The year 2020 appears as text or is clearly invoked, as in a Year of the Rat greeting or a pandemic picture that names the year. Work that merely dates from 2020 is not tagged.

entries.name: numbered
entries.description: A picture belonging to a numbered series shows its own number, such as #4 or 11/40. Not for page numbers, panel numbers or numbering that appears only in the commentary; a date is [dated](#dated) instead.
The year 2019 is written in the picture or referenced, whether through a Year of the Pig [card](#card) or Japan's change from the Heisei era to Reiwa. A creation date alone does not count.
The year 2018 shows up as lettering or as a clear reference, often a Year of the Dog greeting. Simply being made that year is not a reason to use it.

entries.name: roman_numeral
entries.description: Numbers written in Roman numerals such as IV or XII, on a [clock](#clock) face, a [title](#title) or a character's design. Applies to the numeral itself appearing somewhere in the picture.
The year 2014 appears as lettering or is plainly referenced, often as a Year of the Horse greeting. Merely having been drawn that year is not enough.
The number 2013 is written into the picture or referred to, as on a Year of the Snake [card](#card). Upload and creation dates do not count.

entries.name: timestamp
entries.description: Numbers showing a time or date appear in the picture, whether on a [clock](#clock), a [phone](#phone), a [caption](#caption) like eight hours later, or beside the artist's [signature](#signature). Add [dated](#dated) when it is the artwork's own date.

entries.name: countdown
entries.description: The picture carries a number of days left until a release, [anniversary](#anniversary) or [birthday](#birthday), often written as あとX日. Usually one entry in a series of drawings [counting](#counting) down to the date.
The year 2012 is shown as text or clearly referred to, such as in a Year of the Dragon greeting. Pictures that were simply made in 2012 are not tagged.
The year 2011 is written in the image or referenced by the scene, for instance on a Year of the Rabbit [card](#card). The date of creation on its own does not qualify.
The figures 2010 appear as text or the picture plainly refers to that year, often through a Year of the Tiger greeting. Do not apply it just because the drawing was made then.

entries.name: character_age
entries.description: A character's age appears written in the picture, normally on a [profile](#profile) or reference sheet beside the name. Look for the age markers used in Japanese, Chinese or Korean next to a number.
The year 2009 is written into the picture or clearly referred to, as in a New Year greeting for the Year of the Ox. A work that merely dates from 2009 is not tagged.
Something in the image reads 2006, or the subject refers to that year, which fell under the Dog. Use it for what is depicted, never for the work's own date.

entries.name: height
entries.description: How [tall](#tall) a character is is stated in the picture, as a [figure](#figure) written beside them or a measurement being taken. Several characters lined up for [comparison](#comparison) is [height_chart](#height_chart).
The year 2007 appears as lettering or the picture refers to it, the Year of the Pig. It has nothing to do with when the artist made the piece.
The year 2002 is written somewhere in the image or referenced by what is shown, the Year of the Horse. It is not a way of [recording](#recording) when the piece was drawn.
The number 2008 is written in the picture or the subject matter alludes to that year, which fell under the Rat. A creation date on the image does not count.
The year 2005 is written in the picture or alluded to by the scene, the Year of the Rooster. A date stamp beside the artist's name is [no](#no) reason to apply it.

entries.name: measurements
entries.description: Bodily statistics written directly into the picture, such as [height](#height), [weight](#weight), age or the classic three sizes. Presented as labels beside a [figure](#figure) or as a small data sheet.
The figures 2004 show up in the image, or the content points at that year, the Year of the Monkey. Skip it when the only link is the date the drawing was completed.
The number 2001 appears in the picture or its subject nods to that year, which fell under the Snake. A signed date by itself is not enough.

entries.name: binary
entries.description: Strings of ones and zeroes shown in the picture, generally as shorthand for computers and code. It applies whether or not the digits actually [spell](#spell) anything.

entries.name: episode_number
entries.description: A number identifying an episode is printed in the picture, as on a [title](#title) [card](#card) or a broadcast [caption](#caption). Common in screenshots and in artwork [imitating](#imitating) them.
The picture spells out 2003 or refers to that year, which fell under the Goat in the [zodiac](#zodiac). When the artwork was finished has [no](#no) bearing on it.

entries.name: price
entries.description: A sum of [money](#money) written into the picture, on a [tag](#tag), a [menu](#menu), a signboard or a [screen](#screen). The readable [figure](#figure) is the point.

entries.name: number_pun
entries.description: Digits stand in for syllables to [spell](#spell) out a Japanese word, since each numeral [can](#can) be read several different ways. A date or a [jersey](#jersey) number thereby turns into a name or a phrase.

entries.name: weight
entries.description: A character's weight is stated somewhere in the picture, usually read off a [bathroom](#bathroom) scale or written on a [chart](#chart). The reaction to the number is generally the point of the scene.

entries.name: three_sizes
entries.description: Bust, waist and hip [measurements](#measurements) written into the picture, usually as a set of three numbers on a [profile](#profile) [card](#card) or [chart](#chart).

entries.name: damage_numbers
entries.description: Numerals popping up over a character to report the size of a hit, or the health a heal gave [back](#back). Borrowed from role-playing game interfaces and usually drawn [floating](#floating) upward and [fading](#fading).

entries.name: august
entries.description: The name of the eighth month appears somewhere in the picture, spelled out, written as 八月, or printed on a calendar page. A date given in figures takes [dated](#dated) instead, since the [tag](#tag) wants the word itself.

entries.name: june
entries.description: The name of the sixth month is written in the picture, usually on a calendar or a greeting. A date given in figures belongs to [dated](#dated).

entries.name: july
entries.description: The name of the seventh month is written in the picture, on a calendar page, a [card](#card) or a [caption](#caption). Dates given in figures belong to [dated](#dated).

entries.name: chapter_number
entries.description: A number printed on the illustration announcing that a new chapter begins here, generally across a [title](#title) page. It labels the installment rather than [counting](#counting) [pages](#pages).

entries.name: equation
entries.description: Mathematical [working](#working) — symbols, numbers and an equals [sign](#sign) — on a blackboard, on [paper](#paper) or [floating](#floating) in the air. It also covers playful sums that add characters or feelings together.

entries.name: april
entries.description: The name of the fourth month is written in the picture, spelled out in any language or [standing](#standing) as the numeral heading a calendar. A full numeric date belongs to the [dated](#dated) [tag](#tag) instead.

entries.name: december
entries.description: The twelfth month named outright in the picture, on a calendar page, a [card](#card) or a [birthday](#birthday) [note](#note). Japanese writes it as a month numeral, while a full numeric date belongs to [dated](#dated) instead.

entries.name: november
entries.description: The name of the month appears written in the picture, spelled out in letters or as juuichigatsu, often on a calendar or a [birthday](#birthday) greeting. A bare numeric date does not count.

entries.name: october
entries.description: The name of the tenth month appears written in the picture, spelled out in letters or in Japanese, on a calendar, a greeting or a [caption](#caption). A date given only in numbers takes [dated](#dated) instead.

entries.name: march
entries.description: The month named in the picture, on a calendar page, a greeting or a [caption](#caption), spelled out or written as the Japanese characters. A numeric date such as 3/14 takes [dated](#dated) instead.

entries.name: february
entries.description: The name of the second month appears in the picture, spelled out or written as the number of the month on a calendar. A full numeric date such as 2/14/2012 is not this.

entries.name: january
entries.description: The name of the first month is written in the picture, on a calendar page, a greeting or a [caption](#caption). A date given in figures belongs to [dated](#dated) instead.

entries.name: counting
entries.description: A character works through a count, usually on their fingers, sometimes with the numbers drawn beside them. The counting matters more than what is being counted.

entries.name: september
entries.description: The name of the ninth month appears in the picture, written out or given in Japanese as kugatsu, or marked on a calendar. A numeric date such as 9/14 belongs to the [dated](#dated) [tag](#tag) instead.

entries.name: clockshow
entries.description: A [clock](#clock) or digital [display](#display) in the frame shows a readable time, usually in a screenshot or an imitation of one. The point is that the exact hour [can](#can) be made out.
The year 2000 is written into the picture or invoked by its content, often as a Year of the Dragon greeting. The work's own creation date is not what this records.
The biblical number of the beast is written or displayed somewhere in the picture. It usually signals something demonic or occult, or is played for deliberate edge.
The figures 1996 appear written in the picture, or the scene points at that year some other way. A date [sitting](#sitting) beside the artist's [signature](#signature) is not reason enough to use it.
Something in the picture reads 1998, or the subject alludes to that year. It describes what is shown, not the date on which the artist made the work.
The number 1999 is written into the picture or the scene refers to that year. A creation date on the drawing does not qualify on its own.

entries.name: http_status_code
entries.description: A web error number such as [404](#404) is written into the picture, usually as a joke about something being missing. The code itself is the visible text.

entries.name: temperature
entries.description: A temperature [reading](#reading) appears in the picture, on a [thermometer](#thermometer), a digital [display](#display) or written out in degrees. Fever readings and weather figures are the common cases.
The year 1997 is spelled out somewhere in the image, or the content refers to it. Recording when the picture happened to be finished is not what this is for.

entries.name: artist_name
entries.description: The artist's name or [handle](#handle) appears somewhere on the picture. A handwritten [signature](#signature) also takes signature, and a social-media handle its own [tag](#tag).

entries.name: signature
entries.description: A visible signature on the image, usually the artist's, sometimes a voice actor's or an in-story autograph. Frequently appears together with [dated](#dated).

entries.name: twitter_username
entries.description: Text on the image [giving](#giving) a social-media [handle](#handle), normally the artist's, [serving](#serving) as a [signature](#signature). Also covers other [platform](#platform) handles when used the same way; check the artist's own listed profiles to confirm.

entries.name: dated
entries.description: The date the work was made is written somewhere on the picture, usually next to the artist's name. Do not add a year [tag](#tag) for it unless the picture is about that year; a date written only in the commentary is dated_commentary, and a date shown inside the scene is [timestamp](#timestamp).

entries.name: watermark
entries.description: Text or a [logo](#logo) overlaid on the image to identify the creator or mark a paid-reward sample. Add [watermark_grid](#watermark_grid) when it [tiles](#tiles) most of the picture.

entries.name: copyright_name
entries.description: The [title](#title) of the series, game or film the picture belongs to, written somewhere in it. Any language, any abbreviation, and mangled spellings or odd romanisations all qualify.

entries.name: logo
entries.description: A company or copyright logo, real or invented, worked into the picture or imitated by it. A recognisable mark deliberately altered is [logo_parody](#logo_parody) instead.

entries.name: web_address
entries.description: A URL such as www.example.com is written somewhere in the picture, typically as an artist's [watermark](#watermark) or [signature](#signature) line.

entries.name: artist_logo
entries.description: A mark or [emblem](#emblem) an artist uses to [sign](#sign) their work, sometimes built out of their initials. Often placed beside a written name or a date.

entries.name: page_number
entries.description: A number printed in the [corner](#corner) or margin, marking a page's place in a [book](#book), [comic](#comic) or magazine. Usually a [sign](#sign) that the image is a [scan](#scan) or a page from a self-published comic.

entries.name: copyright_notice
entries.description: A line of small print declaring ownership, usually [carrying](#carrying) a copyright or registered trademark symbol beside a company name. Common on official and promotional artwork; it marks the printed line itself, not who owns the work.

entries.name: sample_watermark
entries.description: The word SAMPLE, or its Japanese equivalent, stamped across the picture as a [watermark](#watermark), usually to stop [merchandise](#merchandise) previews being copied. Tagged with watermark.

entries.name: weibo_watermark
entries.description: A [watermark](#watermark) identifying an account on a Chinese social [platform](#platform), automatically added by the site to some uploads. It typically sits beside the platform's [logo](#logo).

entries.name: company_name
entries.description: A company's name or [logo](#logo) is visible somewhere on the picture, such as a publisher's mark. The [title](#title) of the series itself is [copyright_name](#copyright_name).

entries.name: weibo_logo
entries.description: The [logo](#logo) of a Chinese social [platform](#platform) appears in the picture, usually as part of a [watermark](#watermark) stamped on an upload from that site.

entries.name: content_rating
entries.description: An age or content rating mark is visible on the picture, such as an R-18 notice on a doujinshi [cover](#cover), a rating board [label](#label), or wording reserving the work for adults.

entries.name: copyright_logo
entries.description: A rights holder's [logo](#logo) stamped onto the picture, usually small and tucked near an edge. Typical of official and promotional artwork.

entries.name: milestone_celebration
entries.description: An artist's thank-you illustration for [reaching](#reaching) a follower or view-count milestone, with the number shown in the background, on a [sign](#sign), or written on a character. Usually paired with a message thanking viewers and subscribers.

entries.name: instagram_username
entries.description: The artist has written their Instagram [handle](#handle) onto the picture, usually in a [corner](#corner) and often next to the [platform](#platform) [logo](#logo). It marks the credit, not anything happening in the scene.

entries.name: fanbox_username
entries.description: A line of text points to the artist's page on a subscription [platform](#platform). A credit line of the same sort as [twitter_username](#twitter_username), not ordinary lettering inside the scene.

entries.name: deviantart_username
entries.description: The artist's DeviantArt [handle](#handle) written onto the picture, [pointing](#pointing) viewers to their account. One of the username marks alongside [twitter_username](#twitter_username) and [pixiv_username](#pixiv_username).

entries.name: product_placement
entries.description: A recognisable real brand name or product has been placed in the scene on purpose as advertising, such as a labelled [drink](#drink) [can](#can) or a [branded](#branded) [storefront](#storefront). Distinct from an incidental [logo](#logo); the commercial intent is what counts.

entries.name: title
entries.description: The name of a series or work is written into the illustration, as on a doujinshi [cover](#cover). A copyright holder's name belongs to [copyright_name](#copyright_name) instead.

entries.name: pixiv_id
entries.description: The artist's numeric member ID is written somewhere on the picture. A chosen [handle](#handle) written instead is [pixiv_username](#pixiv_username).

entries.name: pixiv_username
entries.description: The artist's chosen [handle](#handle) is written on the picture. The automatically assigned numeric ID written instead is [pixiv_id](#pixiv_id).

entries.name: circle_name
entries.description: The name of the artist's doujin group is written somewhere on the picture, sometimes beside the artist's own name. A band or other non-illustrating group's name is [group_name](#group_name).

entries.name: too_many_watermarks
entries.description: Several watermarks plastered over the image, enough to be obvious even at thumbnail size and to spoil the picture.

entries.name: instagram_logo
entries.description: The rounded-square [camera](#camera) mark of Instagram appears somewhere in the frame, most often beside a [handle](#handle) the artist has signed with. It frequently accompanies [instagram_username](#instagram_username).

entries.name: commissioner_name
entries.description: The name of whoever commissioned the picture, or of the person it was made as a [gift](#gift) for, is written on the image itself. Commission platforms that add it by default are the usual source.

entries.name: pixiv_logo
entries.description: The site [logo](#logo) appears somewhere in the picture, usually beside the artist's written ID or [handle](#handle) as a credit. Add [pixiv_id](#pixiv_id) or [pixiv_username](#pixiv_username) for the text [sitting](#sitting) next to it.

entries.name: watermark_grid
entries.description: A [watermark](#watermark) repeated in a regular pattern across the whole picture rather than tucked into one [corner](#corner). Preview or sample watermarks often take this form.

entries.name: tumblr_username
entries.description: Text on the picture naming an account on a specific blogging [platform](#platform), usually the artist's own [handle](#handle) [standing](#standing) in for a [signature](#signature). Check the linked artist entry to confirm the [profile](#profile) actually [matches](#matches).

entries.name: logo_parody
entries.description: A well-known [logo](#logo) reworked to [suit](#suit) the picture's joke or to sidestep the trademark, as when the M of a fast-food [sign](#sign) becomes a W. It often accompanies [brand_name_imitation](#brand_name_imitation).

entries.name: facebook_username
entries.description: A line of text in the artwork gives the artist's social network account. It is a credit line of the same kind as [twitter_username](#twitter_username) and is not counted as ordinary text in the scene.

entries.name: character_signature
entries.description: The work looks as though one of the characters in it signed the picture, rather than the artist. The [signature](#signature) belongs to the fiction.

entries.name: credits
entries.description: A [list](#list) naming the [people](#people), groups or [tools](#tools) behind a work, as in an end roll or a [staff](#staff) listing. Text about how the picture was made rather than part of its scene.

entries.name: credits_page
entries.description: The page of a self-published [book](#book) that names [everyone](#everyone) who worked on it. Mostly [plain](#plain) text, and usually near the [back](#back).

entries.name: bluesky_username
entries.description: The poster's [handle](#handle) on a microblogging service written into the picture, generally small and tucked into a [corner](#corner). It [credits](#credits) where the work was published and says nothing about what is drawn.

entries.name: seal_impression
entries.description: The red stamped mark of a name seal pressed onto a picture, usually a [square](#square) or oblong block of characters. Across East Asia it does the work a [signature](#signature) does elsewhere.

entries.name: stamp_mark
entries.description: The [ink](#ink) impression a stamp leaves behind, pressed onto [paper](#paper), a document, or someone's skin. Reads as a hard-edged shape, most often round or [square](#square).

entries.name: deviantart_logo
entries.description: The DeviantArt [logo](#logo) drawn into the picture, generally next to the artist's [handle](#handle) on that site. One of the marks that says where the artist posts.

entries.name: alpha_signature
entries.description: A [signature](#signature) or [handle](#handle) hidden in the [transparent](#transparent) part of a [file](#file) rather than painted into the artwork. It stays [invisible](#invisible) against a matching background and shows up pale against any other.

entries.name: email_address
entries.description: An address for electronic [mail](#mail) is written somewhere in the picture, often beside a [signature](#signature) or on a [card](#card) or [screen](#screen). Usually a contact detail rather than part of the scene itself.

entries.name: lofter_username
entries.description: The artist's [handle](#handle) on the Lofter [platform](#platform) written into the artwork, [pointing](#pointing) viewers to that account. It sits alongside a [signature](#signature) or artist name rather than replacing one.

entries.name: company_logo
entries.description: The mark of a company, real or invented, appears somewhere in the picture, on packaging, a shopfront, a [screen](#screen) or a garment. It identifies a brand rather than the artist.

entries.name: artstation_username
entries.description: The artist's ArtStation [handle](#handle) written into the picture, naming where their gallery [can](#can) be found. Usually placed with a [signature](#signature) or a [logo](#logo).

entries.name: character_watermark
entries.description: An artist marks the work with a small drawing of a character who has nothing to do with the picture, using it as a personal sign-off. Those [cameo](#cameo) figures are normally left untagged so searches stay clean.

entries.name: the_end_(phrase)
entries.description: The words that close a story, written into the picture in English or as the French Fin. They usually sit on a final panel or over a [fading](#fading) scene.

entries.name: character_logo
entries.description: A [logo](#logo) built around a character's face or [silhouette](#silhouette), [standing](#standing) in for a brand, a group or the work itself. It sits on the image as a graphic rather than as an object in the scene.

entries.name: artstation_logo
entries.description: The ArtStation mark placed on the picture, usually tucked into a [corner](#corner) beside a [handle](#handle) to point at the artist's gallery there. Often sits with a [signature](#signature) or a date.

entries.name: youtube_username
entries.description: A line of text placed in the artwork naming the artist's account on a video-sharing site, usually tucked into a [corner](#corner). It [credits](#credits) the maker instead of describing the picture.

entries.name: twitch_username
entries.description: A line of text in the artwork naming the creator's streaming channel. Sits alongside a [signature](#signature) as a [pointer](#pointer) to where they broadcast.

entries.name: colophon
entries.description: The small block of publishing details printed in a [book](#book) or doujinshi: date, [circle](#circle) or publisher, and [printer](#printer). It usually sits on a [credits](#credits) page near the [back](#back), though it [can](#can) appear on a [cover](#cover) or at the foot of a page.

entries.name: comic
entries.description: Sequential art laid out in panels: manga [pages](#pages), doujinshi, webcomics, four-panel strips. Framing tags such as [straight-on](#straight-on) or [cowboy_shot](#cowboy_shot) are left off unless the whole comic shows a single character.

entries.name: 4koma
entries.description: A four-panel strip laid out as one continuous run, vertically, horizontally or in a [square](#square) block. It is the yonkoma format behind countless [gag](#gag) manga.

entries.name: cover
entries.description: Cover art of any kind, whether genuine or mocked up. Always add the more specific [tag](#tag) as [well](#well): a [book](#book), magazine, album, disc or game cover.

entries.name: cover_page
entries.description: Cover art for printed matter other than magazines, most often self-published books, but also manga volumes, novels, artbooks and calendars. Genuine covers and mock-ups both count.

entries.name: doujin_cover
entries.description: The front page of a self-published [book](#book), usually [carrying](#carrying) a [title](#title) and the circle's name over the artwork. Wide [landscape](#landscape) versions often hold the whole wraparound [jacket](#jacket).

entries.name: 2koma
entries.description: A [comic](#comic) built from two panels on the page, usually stacked one above the other: a setup and its payoff. Longer strips take [3koma](#3koma) or [4koma](#4koma) instead.

entries.name: silent_comic
entries.description: A [comic](#comic) told without written dialogue or [narration](#narration). Speech and thought bubbles, where they appear at all, hold only symbols, punctuation or small pictures.

entries.name: 3koma
entries.description: A three-panel strip read as one continuous run, usually stacked vertically but sometimes laid out across. Count the panels: the four-panel form is [4koma](#4koma).

entries.name: multiple_4koma
entries.description: Two or more four-panel strips share a single image. Artwork outside the strips, such as a character posed beside them, makes [no](#no) difference to the [tag](#tag).

entries.name: 1koma
entries.description: A [comic](#comic) that tells its whole joke inside one self-contained panel, in the manner of a single-panel [newspaper](#newspaper) strip. Full-page spreads, bordered pictures and images that merely borrow speech bubbles or [greyscale](#greyscale) do not qualify.

entries.name: 5koma
entries.description: A five-panel strip [running](#running) continuously down or across the page. It is a less common relative of the four-panel [gag](#gag) format.

entries.name: cover_image
entries.description: The clean version of a [cover](#cover): the artwork alone, without the [title](#title) lettering and logos laid over it. It normally exists alongside the finished cover it was drawn for.

entries.name: text-only_page
entries.description: A page made up entirely of [writing](#writing) with [no](#no) illustration, typically a comic's [afterword](#afterword), [credits](#credits) or [narration](#narration) page.

entries.name: square_4koma
entries.description: A four-panel [comic](#comic) arranged in a two-by-two [grid](#grid) instead of a single [column](#column). The tight layout often needs [numbered](#numbered) panels or arrows to make the [reading](#reading) order clear.

entries.name: left-to-right_manga
entries.description: A Japanese [comic](#comic) laid out so panels, balloons and text run left to right rather than the usual right to left. Comics originally written in a language that reads that way anyway are excluded.

entries.name: manga_cover
entries.description: The front of a [comic](#comic) volume, genuine or mocked up, [carrying](#carrying) the [title](#title), the author's name and [cover](#cover) design. Pages from inside are not this.

entries.name: segmented_comic
entries.description: A [comic](#comic) whose individual panels were posted as separate images rather than as one page, a format common on social media since the 2010s. Not [1koma](#1koma), since each piece belongs to a larger whole, and not a [splash_page](#splash_page).

entries.name: comic_cover
entries.description: The front [cover](#cover) of a western [comic](#comic) [book](#book) or graphic novel, whether genuine or invented. Parody covers [imitating](#imitating) a well-known [title](#title) belong here too.

entries.name: splash_page
entries.description: A full [comic](#comic) page given over to one continuous illustration with [no](#no) panel divisions, used for emphasis within an ongoing story rather than as a stand-alone piece. Some webcomics and one-shots are built entirely from [pages](#pages) like this.

entries.name: right-to-left_comic
entries.description: A [comic](#comic) drawn to be read from right to left, so panels, balloons and text run in the Japanese direction even when the language itself is not Japanese. A cue for readers used to the opposite order.

entries.name: video_game_cover
entries.description: Box art for a console or [computer](#computer) game, either from a real release or invented as a mock-up. Title lettering, a [platform](#platform) [banner](#banner) and rating marks give the layout away.

entries.name: afterword
entries.description: The closing [note](#note) at the end of a [book](#book) or a self-published [comic](#comic), where the author speaks to the reader about how the work came together. A small self-portrait beside the text is common.

entries.name: to_be_continued
entries.description: The closing [caption](#caption) promising the story goes on, set over the final panel or frame. Often played for laughs by freezing an entirely ordinary moment as though it were a cliffhanger.

entries.name: numbered_panels
entries.description: The panels of a [comic](#comic) carry printed numbers telling the reader the order to take them in. It is a [reading](#reading) aid rather than part of the story.

entries.name: back_cover
entries.description: The rear outer page of a [book](#book) or doujinshi, usually a smaller illustration alongside a [circle](#circle) [logo](#logo) or publication details. It belongs with the front [cover](#cover) of the same volume.

entries.name: vertical_comic
entries.description: A [comic](#comic) laid out as one [tall](#tall) [column](#column) of panels meant to be scrolled through rather than read across a page. The webtoon format.

entries.name: 6koma
entries.description: A six-panel strip read as one continuous piece, laid out down, across or as a block. Two separate three-panel strips [sharing](#sharing) a page are not the same thing.

entries.name: blank_page
entries.description: An image showing nothing at all, an empty [field](#field) where the drawing would be. Comics use it for a silent beat, a stretch of time passing, or something left to the reader.

entries.name: title_page
entries.description: The [opening](#opening) page of a [comic](#comic) or a chapter, [carrying](#carrying) its [title](#title) and often the author's name across a decorative illustration.

entries.name: fanbook
entries.description: A self-published fan [comic](#comic) or art booklet, the English word for doujinshi. Used for scans and covers of such books.

entries.name: highres
entries.description: An image of at least 1600 by 1200 pixels, roughly 1.9 megapixels and up. It is applied automatically; bigger files take [absurdres](#absurdres) or [incredibly_absurdres](#incredibly_absurdres), and very small ones [lowres](#lowres).

entries.name: absurdres
entries.description: A very large image, at least 3200 pixels across or 2400 [tall](#tall), roughly eight megapixels and up. Files from 1600 by 1200 upward are [highres](#highres), and anything over ten thousand pixels on a side is [incredibly_absurdres](#incredibly_absurdres).

entries.name: lowres
entries.description: A small picture [measuring](#measuring) [no](#no) more than 500 pixels on either side, roughly a quarter of a megapixel. Larger sizes take [highres](#highres), [absurdres](#absurdres) or [incredibly_absurdres](#incredibly_absurdres) instead.

entries.name: image_sample
entries.description: A shrunk or recompressed copy of a picture, made for faster loading rather than by the artist. It is neither a promotional copy stamped with a sample [watermark](#watermark) nor an alternate size the artist released.

entries.name: resized
entries.description: The image has been scaled from its original dimensions. Always pair it with [downscaled](#downscaled) or [upscaled](#upscaled) to say which way; a picture that has had part cut off is [cropped](#cropped), not resized.

entries.name: incredibly_absurdres
entries.description: A picture at least ten thousand pixels along one side, roughly a hundred megapixels or more. It sits above [absurdres](#absurdres) at the top of the resolution [ladder](#ladder) and is applied automatically.

entries.name: downscaled
entries.description: The picture has been reduced from the size it was made at, either because the original was too large to post or because somebody shrank a version found elsewhere.

entries.name: upscaled
entries.description: An image enlarged beyond its source resolution, usually by someone other than the original artist. The original is generally preferred over such a copy once it turns up.

entries.name: qvga
entries.description: An image sized at the small quarter-VGA resolution of 320 by 240 pixels. Marks output from [old](#old) phones and handheld consoles, and sits far below the modern [highres](#highres) threshold.

entries.name: animated
entries.description: The [file](#file) moves rather than [sitting](#sitting) still, whether as a gif, an animated png, [flash](#flash), [ugoira](#ugoira) or [video](#video). Always add the narrower format [tag](#tag) beside it, such as [animated_gif](#animated_gif) or video.

entries.name: animated_gif
entries.description: A GIF [holding](#holding) more than one frame. A single-frame GIF does not qualify, and one clipped from a broadcast episode should carry [anime_screenshot](#anime_screenshot) too.

entries.name: video
entries.description: The post is a video [file](#file), usually WebM or MP4, rather than a still image or an [animated](#animated) GIF. Long uploads are typically capped at a [couple](#couple) of minutes.

entries.name: sound
entries.description: A [video](#video) or Flash [file](#file) that actually plays audio. Written sound effects drawn into a picture get [sound_effects](#sound_effects) instead; this [tag](#tag) is applied automatically to videos [carrying](#carrying) an audio track.

entries.name: ugoira
entries.description: A custom animation format made of a zip [file](#file) of frames with per-frame timing, played [back](#back) by a dedicated [script](#script). Since each frame carries its own delay, the frame rate [can](#can) vary through the clip.

entries.name: looping_animation
entries.description: An animation whose end runs seamlessly [back](#back) into its beginning, so it appears to have neither. A visible fade or cut between the two does not count.

entries.name: audible_music
entries.description: The file's soundtrack carries [music](#music). It applies only to files that actually play [sound](#sound), and [audible_speech](#audible_speech) goes alongside when [singing](#singing) or [talking](#talking) [can](#can) be made out over the tune.

entries.name: audible_speech
entries.description: Recognisable spoken language [can](#can) be heard in the file's audio. Wordless mouth noises and [plain](#plain) [moaning](#moaning) do not count.

entries.name: flash
entries.description: An animation, game or [music](#music) [video](#video) authored in Adobe Flash and stored as an SWF [file](#file). The format is long dead in browsers and surviving files play [back](#back) through an emulator.

entries.name: idle_animation
entries.description: The short [standing](#standing) loop a game [sprite](#sprite) plays while nobody presses anything: [breathing](#breathing), shifting [weight](#weight), fiddling with a [weapon](#weapon), tugging at hair or [clothes](#clothes). Fan work recreates these small motions.

entries.name: jpeg_artifacts
entries.description: Blocky compression noise and [mosquito](#mosquito) fuzz around high-contrast edges, [plain](#plain) to see at normal viewing size without zooming. It is common where an image has been re-saved by a social [platform](#platform), and not worth tagging when barely visible.

entries.name: bad_anatomy
entries.description: The body is put together wrongly: limbs [bending](#bending) where [no](#no) joint exists, a [torso](#torso) that does not meet the hips, shoulders in impossible places. It is a [note](#note) about the drawing, with narrower tags such as [bad_hands](#bad_hands) and [bad_proportions](#bad_proportions) covering particular parts.

entries.name: artistic_error
entries.description: A genuine slip by the artist: an extra finger, a missing [shadow](#shadow), a [reflection](#reflection) that does not match, the wrong eye colour. Anatomy that is merely drawn badly is [bad_anatomy](#bad_anatomy) or [bad_hands](#bad_hands), and deliberate [distortion](#distortion) for comedy is something else again.

entries.name: adversarial_noise
entries.description: Visible artifacts left by a tool that perturbs a picture to spoil it as machine-learning [training](#training) data, often a faint swirling texture over the surface. It also marks an image known to carry such protection.

entries.name: bad_feet
entries.description: Feet drawn plainly wrong: misshapen, wrongly sized, [toes](#toes) miscounted or joined on at odd angles. It sits among the [family](#family) of drawing-fault [notes](#notes) alongside [bad_hands](#bad_hands).

entries.name: scan_artifacts
entries.description: Visible flaws left by a poor [scan](#scan): warped blur near the binding, print [bleeding](#bleeding) through from the reverse side, [halftone](#halftone) [dots](#dots), shifted or washed-out colours, creases and [dust](#dust) specks. Implies scan.

entries.name: typo
entries.description: An accidental spelling mistake in text within the picture. Broken English written by a non-native [speaker](#speaker) is engrish, a separate [tag](#tag) not to be mixed in with this one.

entries.name: bad_hands
entries.description: Hands have come out wrong: too large or too small for the arm, a thumb of the wrong length, fingers [bending](#bending) where they cannot. A miscounted number of fingers is [extra_digits](#extra_digits) on its own.

entries.name: bad_proportions
entries.description: Parts of the body are the wrong size against one another, a head too small for the shoulders or one arm far longer than its partner. Deliberate stylisation such as [chibi](#chibi) is not what it means.

entries.name: crease
entries.description: A fold line [running](#running) visibly through a scanned picture, left by a page or poster that was [folded](#folded) before it went under the scanner. A flaw of the copy rather than of the artwork.

entries.name: bad_perspective
entries.description: Perspective has been mishandled: [foreshortening](#foreshortening) fails, background lines refuse to converge, or a [figure](#figure) stands at an angle its surroundings contradict. It marks a mistake, not a deliberate [distortion](#distortion).

entries.name: wrong_foot
entries.description: A slip in the drawing where a foot ends up attached to the leg it does not belong to, leaving the [arch](#arch) or big toe facing outward. Counted as an [anatomy](#anatomy) error, not a deliberate design [choice](#choice).

entries.name: bad_leg
entries.description: Legs rendered badly, with [knees](#knees) in impossible places, mismatched lengths, or a shape that does not hold together. Poses [calling](#calling) for [foreshortening](#foreshortening) are where it usually shows.

entries.name: bad_arm
entries.description: One arm has come out wrong, whether unnaturally spindly, jointed where it should not be, or foreshortened into nonsense. It happens most when the artist reaches for an arm stretched toward the viewer.

entries.name: bad_neck
entries.description: The [neck](#neck) has come out too long, too thick, or angled where [no](#no) [spine](#spine) could bend. The head ends up looking [stuck](#stuck) on rather than attached.

entries.name: moire
entries.description: The rippling interference pattern that appears when two fine grids sit over one another: a printed [halftone](#halftone) against a scanner's sampling, or against the pixel [grid](#grid) after resizing. Almost always an artefact of copying rather than something drawn.

entries.name: extra_digits
entries.description: More fingers or [toes](#toes) than there should be. Nearly always a drawing mistake, and a notorious failing of early image generators, though mutants and monsters may have them by design.

entries.name: wrong_hand
entries.description: A slip in the drawing where a hand sits on the arm it does not belong to, so the thumb or palm faces the wrong way. Recorded as an [anatomy](#anatomy) mistake rather than an intentional pose.

entries.name: bad_vulva
entries.description: The vulva is drawn with [anatomy](#anatomy) that does not add up, from misplaced lines to [shapes](#shapes) [no](#no) body has. Futanari work is left out of it, since accuracy is not what it aims at.

entries.name: quality
entries.description: A deliberate, humorous recreation of the mangled art seen in badly [animated](#animated) episodes, drawn to poke fun at cheap production. Japanese fans call the phenomenon yashigani after a notoriously bad episode; a genuine unintended mistake is [artistic_error](#artistic_error) instead.

entries.name: bad_gun_anatomy
entries.description: A firearm drawn so that it could not work or does not resemble the [weapon](#weapon) it stands for: [no](#no) trigger, a bent [barrel](#barrel), a bore wrong for its calibre, whole cartridges [flying](#flying) out. Handling errors such as a reversed magazine, small faults of furniture and deliberately [comic](#comic) sizes are all excluded.

entries.name: bad_reflection
entries.description: What appears in a [mirror](#mirror) or other polished surface fails to match whatever stands in front of it. Where the mismatch is clearly deliberate, [different_reflection](#different_reflection) is the [tag](#tag).

entries.name: bad_face
entries.description: The features sit at proportions that fail even by the stylised standards of the medium, quite apart from big eyes and round faces. Eyes placed too high on the [skull](#skull) and a [nose](#nose) [bridge](#bridge) sunk flat into the head are the usual giveaways.

entries.name: bad_ass
entries.description: The buttocks are drawn with their shape or proportions gone astray. It is strictly a comment on the draughtsmanship and has nothing to do with the slang sense of the phrase.

entries.name: official_art
entries.description: Artwork made by the company or artist [holding](#holding) the rights to the series or character, often [carrying](#carrying) a [logo](#logo) or a copyright line somewhere on it. Fan work that merely imitates that look is [official_style](#official_style).

entries.name: game_cg
entries.description: Artwork or an [animated](#animated) asset lifted straight out of a [video](#video) game, most often a visual novel or adult [title](#title). The same artwork posted by its artist elsewhere does not count.

entries.name: scan
entries.description: A picture digitized from a physical original such as a poster, magazine page or [artbook](#artbook). Only for real scans; a drawing [imitating](#imitating) the look of one is a fake_scan. Add [scan_artifacts](#scan_artifacts) when the scanning left visible flaws.

entries.name: tachi-e
entries.description: A visual-novel style character [sprite](#sprite): a [standing](#standing), forward-facing [figure](#figure) on a [plain](#plain) background, drawn so it [can](#can) be reused with swapped [expressions](#expressions) and [poses](#poses). If [dropping](#dropping) the art onto a random scene with a textbox would pass for a screenshot, it likely qualifies.

entries.name: anime_screenshot
entries.description: A still lifted straight out of an [animated](#animated) episode or film rather than drawn as an illustration. Frames grabbed from games or visual novels use screenshot instead.

entries.name: settei
entries.description: Studio reference sheets from an anime production, showing a character or prop from several angles with [measurements](#measurements) and [notes](#notes) for the animators. Working line art rather than a finished picture.

entries.name: fake_screenshot
entries.description: The picture is drawn to look like a capture from a [video](#video) game, a software interface or a [television](#television) programme, interface elements included. It is an illustration, not a real capture; a whole-picture [phone](#phone) [screen](#screen) is [fake_phone_screenshot](#fake_phone_screenshot).

entries.name: promotional_art
entries.description: Artwork made to advertise an anime, manga, game, or doujin release, such as a [key](#key) visual, magazine spread, or [announcement](#announcement) image. Almost always an official production; combine with the franchise's own tags.

entries.name: subtitled
entries.description: A screenshot, or a picture styled to look like one, [carrying](#carrying) subtitle text along the bottom edge. Applies to real screencaps and to [fake_screenshot](#fake_screenshot) pictures alike.

entries.name: artist_collaboration
entries.description: More than one artist worked on the same picture, for instance one drawing the lines and another colouring them. It does not mean characters from different series meeting, which is a [crossover](#crossover).

entries.name: novel_illustration
entries.description: An official illustration printed inside a novel, such as the colour plates and [interior](#interior) pictures of a light novel. It records where the picture came from.

entries.name: concept_art
entries.description: Design work made during production of a game, film or animation to settle a character, a setting or a mood before the final version. Usually official, and often annotated.

entries.name: official_wallpaper
entries.description: A desktop or [phone](#phone) wallpaper released by the rights holder, traditionally from the downloads page of a series site. It is a kind of official art and normally comes in a screen-shaped ratio.

entries.name: album_cover
entries.description: Cover artwork for a [music](#music) release, real or invented, laid out as a [square](#square) sleeve and often [carrying](#carrying) a [title](#title). Only the artwork counts; a disc case drawn as an object inside a scene is [cd_case](#cd_case), and a [book](#book) of photographs is [photo_album](#photo_album).

entries.name: magazine_scan
entries.description: A scanned page from inside a printed periodical rather than its front. Paper texture, [halftone](#halftone) [dots](#dots) and columns of print usually give it away.

entries.name: magazine_cover
entries.description: The front page of a periodical, genuine or invented, [carrying](#carrying) the [title](#title), [cover](#cover) lines and a good deal of small text around the artwork. Pages from inside are [magazine_scan](#magazine_scan) instead.

entries.name: cosplay_photo
entries.description: A photograph of a real person in [costume](#costume) rather than a drawing. Tag the character being portrayed alongside it.

entries.name: real_life_insert
entries.description: A real person, such as a friend, relative, actor, or [politician](#politician), has been drawn into the picture, either as themselves, as an original character [standing](#standing) in for them, or through an existing character used as their persona.

entries.name: artbook
entries.description: Artwork taken from a printed collection of illustrations, whether official material or an artist's own [book](#book). Tag [scan](#scan) where the page has been scanned.

entries.name: fake_phone_screenshot
entries.description: The whole picture imitates a [phone](#phone) [screen](#screen): a [lock](#lock) screen, a chat [thread](#thread), a [camera](#camera) view. Where a phone screen merely appears somewhere inside a scene, use [cellphone_photo](#cellphone_photo).

entries.name: calendar_(medium)
entries.description: The picture is a page from a printed calendar, generally a [scan](#scan) showing the artwork together with its month [grid](#grid). A calendar appearing inside a scene is [calendar_(object)](#calendar_(object)).
